newsitem.title: UK: Paisley tells N.Ireland Protestants "no surrender".
newsitem.headline: Paisley tells N.Ireland Protestants "no surrender".

text.p: Northern Ireland's most outspoken politician, Ian Paisley, told the next British government on Friday that Protestants would not give up their "birthright" to parade through Catholic areas.

Paisley served notice to the government which wins May 1 elections that hardline Protestants were in no mood to negotiate with minority Catholics on parades which last year lit the fuse to the worst civil unrest in the province for decades.
"We will walk the roads of Ulster (Northern Ireland). We will march to our places of worship. We will not surrender an inch to Dublin or to Poperey," he said to long applause.

Paisley rejected appeals by church leaders, police and government officials that Protestant Orders negotiate alternative routes to avoid offending Catholics at this year's marching season, which began peacefully last Monday.
By addressing the rally Paisley became the most senior person of the Northern Ireland Protestant political establishment to throw his weight behind moves to refuse to negotiate disputed marches.

The Orange Order, which is heavily involved in the marches, is showing signs of a split between moderates who want to avoid confrontation with the security forces and Catholics and hardliners who oppose any deals to re-route parades.
Police fear that this year's marches could be as disputed and as violent as last year's as Protestants and Catholics seek to make their political points to the next British government.

Paisley was speaking less than a mile (two km) from the site at Drumcree church where thousands of Protestants confronted a massive police cordon last July to protest against a ban on their parade through the Catholic Garvaghy Road area.
Protestant fury at a police ban on the parade crippled the province until the ban was lifted; then Catholic fury was ignited and burned for several days.

Paisley ridiculed Roman Catholicism and Sinn Fein, political wing of IRA guerrillas whose hand he saw in residents' groups in Portadown and elsewhere trying to deny Protestants a right to march, which they trace back for centuries.
"Things are getting pretty strange if people who have walked for 180 years are told 'you cannot march until you get agreement with a bunch of IRA murderers'," he said.

Paisley, head of the small Democratic Unionist Party, which has three seats in the British parliament, said moves to deny Protestants the right to march through Catholic areas were an attempt to appease the Dublin government and the IRA.
The party is the most outspoken opponent of a 1985 agreement between Ireland and Britain which gives the Dublin government a say in the running of the province's affairs.

Paisley said moves to deny Protestants the right to parade behind bands every summer to their places of worship was a denial of human rights aimed ultimately at forcing them to accept the IRA's goal of an end to British rule.
"To Roman Catholics I say: 'You will not breed us out, you will not burn us out or bring us down'," he said.
Paisley was speaking after the IRA claimed responsibility for two bomb warnings which paralysed central Britain's motorway network and cost millions of pounds (dollars).

Sinn Fein has cast doubt on media speculation that the IRA will call a truce shortly in the hope that if the opposition Labour party wins elections it will invite Sinn Fein for talks. Sinn Fein is barred from the talks because of IRA violence.
